sections.overview: The Far Eastern Curlew is a very large migratory shorebird of the East Asian–Australasian flyway.
sections.identification: Its exceptionally long, down-curved bill and dark rump distinguish it; it is bulkier and longer-billed than the Whimbrel (Numenius phaeopus), while the Little Curlew (N. minutus) is much smaller.
sections.habitat: It breeds in north-eastern Asia and winters on coastal mudflats and estuaries from South-East Asia to Australia.
sections.diet: On Australian non-breeding grounds it probes mud for invertebrates, with crabs an important prey.
sections.behavior: It makes long seasonal migrations and depends on a chain of coastal feeding and stopover sites along the flyway.
sections.reproduction: It nests in northern Asia, where accounts describe a ground nest and a typical clutch of four eggs.
sections.ecology: Large intertidal flats, especially stopover areas around the Yellow Sea, are vital to its migration; the related Eurasian Curlew (N. arquata) is smaller and has a white rump, as described in its profile.
sections.conservation: BirdLife and Australian authorities classify it as Critically Endangered, citing decline and loss or degradation of coastal mudflats.
